name: Yeni
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct Bantoid variety known essentially from a remembered song/wordlist (Connell & Zeitlyn 2000); no phonological description of stress.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page yeni1253 (refs: Connell & Zeitlyn 2000; Connell 2017, Language history and language contact in the Mambiloid region of Cameroon, in Beyer & Kramer eds., Frankfurter Afrikanistische Blaetter 24, Koeppe, pp. 111-129; Ethnologue 28).https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/yeni1253
sources.note: Bibliographic only; no descriptive (grammar/phonology) reference for Yeni exists in Glottolog.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce, David Zeitlyn, Sascha Griffiths, Laura Hayward & Marieke Martin. 2021. Language ecology, language endangerment, and relict languages: Case studies from Adamawa (Cameroon-Nigeria). Open Linguistics 7(1): 244-300. doi:10.1515/opli-2021-0011 (CC-BY; downloaded via Internet Archive copy of the De Gruyter PDF)
sources.note: Nothing on Yeni phonology. Only mention is fn. 27, p. 263: 'As well as Yeni, another language whose existence is known through mention in a song but little more survives than the name; see Connell (1998). Gausset (2010) identifies its (former) speakers as the Yeka, now absorbed by the Kwanja.' The word 'stress' occurs once, non-technically.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2007. Endangered languages in Central Africa. In Matthias Brenzinger (ed.), Language Diversity Endangered, 163-178. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.note: Survey chapter; snippet confirms Yeni is extinct and known from remembered songs. Would only supersede the 1997/1998 text if it adds song data.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce & David Zeitlyn. 2000. Njerep: A postcard from the edge. Studies in African Linguistics 29(1): 95-125. doi:10.32473/sal.v29i1.107370
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Phonology section (4.1-4.4) is for Njerep only (three level tones; no stress/accent mention). On Yeni, p. 103: 'Both Kasabe and Yeni are now extinct.. Of Yeni, only a song survives to attest its former existence [Connell 1998]'; p. 115: 'of Yeni barely a whisper.'

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 1997. Moribund languages of the Nigeria-Cameroon borderland. Symposium on Language Endangerment in Africa, Leipzig (conference text of Connell 1998, Brenzinger ed., Endangered Languages in Africa, Koeppe, pp. 207-225).http://mambila.info/Connell/Mori/Moribundlngs.html
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.7 'Yeni': known only through a song; words from the song show it was closely related to Cambap, Njerep and Kasabe; grouped as the 'Yeni-Kasabe cluster' within East Mambila (sec. 3.1). Zero hits for stress/accent/tone in the whole paper.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 1997. The integrity of Mambiloid. Paper presented at WOCAL 2, Leipzig (later in Wolff & Gensler eds. 2000, Proceedings of the 2nd World Congress of African Linguistics).http://mambila.info/Connell/Integ/Integrity.html
sources.note: Comparative Mambiloid phonology (tone systems of two to four levels, vowel harmony, lateral flap); no stress/accent anywhere. Yeni named once: Cambap, Njerep, Langa, Kasabe and Yeni '(the latter two now extinct) likely formed a separate group within East Mambila'. No Yeni data.
Nothing; says all that remains of the language is a song remembered by some Sandani speakers, closely related to Cambap, Njerep and Kasabe.
